match.reason: No bank point teaches the gains from trade itself: the liberalisation card covers the effects of cutting protection, the free trade agreement card covers which countries deals apply to, and the specialisation card covers division of labour within an economy, so none is the same idea at the right depth.

draft.title: Gains from trade
card: Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services between countries. Both sides can gain, because each can buy what it makes less well from a country that makes it better.
Prices and choice
imports can be cheaper than local goods, and households can buy products that are not made at home. Lower prices also help firms that buy imported inputs.
Resources and scale
trade gives access to resources a country lacks. Selling to the world also lets firms make more, which can lower the cost of each unit (economies of scale).
Competition
imports push local firms to compete. Firms that want to keep their customers may cut costs and improve quality, which can raise efficiency.
draft.remember: Trade can lower prices, widen choice, supply resources, allow larger-scale production and push firms to be efficient.

a.q: An Australian bakery sells more bread to Asian markets and its cost per loaf falls as output grows. Which gain from trade is this?
a.why: A larger market lets the bakery make more, and the cost of each loaf falls as output grows. That is an economy of scale. It is not choice or competition, because no new products or rival imports are involved.
a.clue: Think about what happens to cost per unit as output rises.

b.q: Cheap imported tyres arrive in Australia. Local tyre maker Sam's Tyres in Geelong cuts its costs and improves its quality to keep customers. Which gain from trade does this show?
opts: Access to resources not found locally
Economies of scale from export sales
Lower prices from cheaper imported inputs
b.why: The imports push the local firm to compete, so it cuts costs and lifts quality. That is competition leading to efficiency. Lower prices for buyers are a result of the imports, but the firm's response to rivals is the gain shown here.
b.clue: Look at how the local firm reacts to the imports.

problems.detail: The first bullet says each country gains by buying 'what it makes less well from a country that makes it better'. That describes absolute advantage. The gain from trade rests on comparative advantage, meaning lower opportunity cost. A country can gain even when another makes everything better. Year 12 students could take the wrong idea from this.

The stem says cost per loaf falls as output grows, which is the card's definition of economies of scale almost word for word. The clue repeats it again. The question tests matching a definition rather than understanding, so it is easy for Year 12.

proposal.title: Gains from trade
card: Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services between countries. Each country gains by specialising in what it makes at a lower opportunity cost (what it gives up to make it). This is comparative advantage, and it holds even when another country makes everything better.
Prices and choice
imports can be cheaper than local goods, and households can buy products that are not made at home. Lower prices also help firms that buy imported inputs.
Resources and scale
trade gives access to resources a country lacks. Selling to the world also lets firms make more, which can lower the cost of each unit (economies of scale).
Competition
imports push local firms to compete. Firms that want to keep their customers may cut costs and improve quality, which can raise efficiency.
proposal.remember: Trade can lower prices, widen choice, supply resources, allow larger-scale production and push firms to be efficient.

a.q: A small Victorian winery starts exporting to Asia, and its sales triple. Which gain from trade is it most likely to get?
a.why: Exporting gives the winery a much larger market, so it can produce more, which can lower the cost of each bottle. That is economies of scale. More competition from imports does not fit, because the winery is selling abroad, not facing new rival imports at home.
a.clue: What can a firm do with a much larger market?
